⚙️ Brief Introduction to Function Components

Last workbook we saw our first few functions: e.g.,
print()
,
type()
and
len()
. This workbook, you’ll be introduced to a whole slew of them to work with data. Before we dive into those, it’s useful for us to discuss what a function is, and what it does. We’ll go into much more detail next week, so here we discuss what you need to use functions.
To get a function to do its job, you "call" it, that’s what we did here:
Python
Copy
print(...)
​
There are three core components to a function:
the name of the function,
the parameters (if any),
the value it returns (if any).
When using functions, the idea is that you do not need to have knowledge about how a function performs its action, you just need these three things to work with it. We know the name of
type()
, we know the parameters (it takes some input), and we know what it returns (it outputs the type of the input). We don’t know the steps inside the code, and it might not even be informative if we looked at it. We know what it does though!

📛 Function Name

Each function has a name. Like a variable name, a function name may consist of letters, digits, and underscores, and cannot start with a digit. Almost all standard Python functions consist only of lower case letters. Usually a function name expresses concisely what action the function takes. In the previous workbook, we looked at this line of code for example:
JavaScript
Copy
volume_of_cone = pi * radius * radius * height / 3
​
If you would come across a function that’s appropriately named to do the above, it would be something like
calculate_cone_volume()
, which gives us information about what the function does and maybe even what we can expect about the output (calculate = numbers).

🎛️ Parameters & Arguments

Most functions are called with parameters, which are often optional (i.e. you can use the function without providing any, or all arguments). The arguments are placed between the parentheses that follow the function name. If there are multiple parameters, you place commas between them.
🤔
What’s the difference between a parameter and an argument? Parameters are all input options available, arguments are the subset which you actually pass when calling it.
When we call a function, we use some appropriate arguments (again, if the function requires them). In our previous example, the parameters might be
radius
and
height
. With
print()
the parameters are strings:
Python
Copy
volume_of_cone = calculate_cone_volume(radius=3, height=5) # and print("something") print("something", "something else")
​
After we call a function, we expect something to happen.
print()
displays something, our
calculate_cone_volume
calculates something, and outputs a
float
, which is then stored in the variable
volume_of_cone
in the code above.
The arguments are the values that the user supplies to the function to work with. For instance, the
int()
function must be called with one argument, the
print()
function may be called with any number of arguments, which it will display, after which it will go to a new line:
Python
Copy
print(5) print(5 * 2) print() # no parameters! print("parameter")
​
Notice that parameters may be named as well. In the
calculate_cone_volume
example, we pass
radius
and
height
by name with a little
=
for the value (
radius=3, height=5
). The more detailed reasons for this we’ll cover in a later workbook. For now, they’re just handy visual references so we know where we put what.

📤 Return Value

A function may or may not "return" (output) something. If a function returns a value, that value can be used in your code. For instance, the function
int()
returns an integer representation of the parameter it gets. You can place this return value in a variable, using an assignment:
Python
Copy
x = int(2.0)
​
… or use it in a different manner, for instance immediately print it. You can even do nothing with it (although there is usually little reason to call the function in that case).
Python
Copy
x = 2.1 y = '3' z = int(x) print(z) print(int(y)) int(x) # this does nothing
​
As you can see from the example above, and as we have seen before, you can even ‘nest’ function calls as input to another function. The second time we use
print()
, a call to the function
int()
is passed as a parameter. Here,
int()
will be executed before the
print()
function is called, as the Python interpreter first resolves the values for all the parameters before it makes a function call.
Now that we know a bit more about functions, let’s dive into using them to process data!

📑 Working with Files

Last workbook, we have looked at all the basic data types that Python has to offer. However, in all of the scripts we wrote, we defined the data ourselves. Pretty odd, because that’s really not how programming typically works. Data always comes from somewhere; be it a direct user of your software, someone sending requests through a website, or from actual data on your disk! In this workbook, we’ll dive into the magic world of reading datasets using 🐼 Pandas. First, however, it’s useful to learn a bit about the basic file handling functionality in Python. This is a pretty elaborate topic, and (like our data types as well) interacts with all the fancier programming tools we’ll discuss in later workbooks. For now, we’ll just stick to opening files, making some edits (e.g. doing cleaning / preprocessing), and then saving those changes.

🥞 Flat Text Files

When programmers refer to "text files" or "flat text files", they mean files in which all characters are meant to be read as regular characters, like you would type on a keyboard. For instance,
.py
files are flat text files, as are HTML files. Word processor (
.docx
etc.) documents, for example, are not flat text files, and neither are images (e.g.,
.jpg
,
.png
). If you want to know whether a file is a text file or not, you can try to open it in VSCode. If you see only readable text, the file is likely to be a text file. If you see a garbled mess of symbols, it is a so-called "binary file".
Text files consist of lines of text. At the end of a line, there is a "newline" symbol, which in Python is the character
"\n"
as you may remember. Different operating systems use slightly different ways of storing this character in a text file: some Windows programs store it as "carriage return", as well as "line feed" (
"\r\n"
, sometimes thought as a leftover from old typewriters), while on Linux it is always stored as a single
"\n"
. As long as you access a file from Python as a regular text file, Python will convert the characters that it reads to the standard
"\n"
, and vice versa when it writes. So you do not usually need to worry about such differences (except when you need to transfer text files between operating systems, then you might be in trouble 🙂).

💾 Buffering

When you make changes to files, these often are not stored in the files immediately. Instead, the operating system "buffers" the changes in memory, and "flushes" the buffers to the actual files when it sees a need for that. You can force the flushing of the buffers by closing a file. Buffers are also flushed when your program ends normally.
However, when your program crashes (for instance because of a runtime error), buffers might not be flushed, and your files will not be updated to the point where the crash took place. So you cannot take the file contents into account when trying to debug a program. Good opening and closing practice is important, as well as storing the input somewhere. We’ll discuss these here.

🏗️ File Handles, Actions, and Methods

When you work with a file in a program, you have to open the file. Opening a file provides a so-called "file handle". A file handle can be seen as an access point to the file. It contains a "pointer" that indicates a particular place in the file (kind of like the cursor that shows while typing in/moving through file in an editor). That pointer is used when you read from or write to the file. For instance, when you read from the file, it starts reading at the pointer (similar to how we might traverse a string), and moves the pointer forward in the file.
When you open a file, the pointer is placed at a particular spot in the file, depending on how you opened the file. If you opened the file for reading only, the pointer is placed at the start of the file. The same is true when you open the file for both reading and writing. If you open the file for "appending" (i.e., to place new data at the file's end), the file pointer is positioned at the end of the file. Lastly, if you open a file for writing only, the file is actually completely emptied (‼️) and the file pointer is placed at the start of the, now empty, file. To create a new file (i.e., a file with a name that does not exist yet), you open it for "writing only".
After opening the file, the file handle is the only access point. We generally bind it to a variable name; all actions you perform on the file, you perform as methods for the file handle. This is similar to how you can map a
str
to a variable name, and it then has methods like
split
.
💡
Note that any operating system only allows a limited number of files to be open simultaneously. Therefore you should close files that you no longer need to work with. You might run into strange behavior or accidentally wiped files if you don’t!
The file pointer, that indicates where in a file you are working, is moved automatically. For instance, when you read 10 characters from a file, the file pointer indicates which is the first of those 10 characters, and, while reading, moves up 10 characters, so that its new position is 10 characters further in the file than before. When you deal with text files, the automatic movements of the file pointer are exactly what you want. You can position the file pointer manually using specific methods, but such methods are, in general, only used when dealing with binary files (which we won’t have to deal with in this course).

📂 Opening a File Using
open()

To open a file, you use the
open()
function:
Built-in Functions
The Python interpreter has a number of functions and types built into it that are always available. They are listed here in alphabetical order.,,,, Built-in Functions,,, A, abs(), aiter(), all(), a...
https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#open
For now, we’ll discuss two of the input arguments, of which the second one is optional. The first input to this function is the path to the file, formatted as a
str
. For the foreseeable future, to simplify matters, we’ll assume files are in the same directory as our working directory. This means the target file and your
.py
script are in the same directory, which is also the directory that VSCode has open (if you’re brave enough to diverge from that, the 🗄️ Directories bonus content is for you). Hence, for now we’ll just use the name of the file (e.g.,
"some_filename.txt"
) and no paths (e.g.
"../data/some_filename.txt"
). The second argument is the "mode". The mode indicates how you want to treat the file, and is passed as a
str
. There are more options in the docs—these are relevant for now:
Character
Meaning
'r'
open for reading (default)
'w'
open for writing, truncating the file first
'x'
open for exclusive creation, failing if the file already exists
'a'
open for writing, appending to the end of file if it exists
'b'
binary mode
The default mode (which is picked when you do not supply the second argument) is opening the file as a text file for reading only (
'r'
). How you set other modes is discussed later.
The
open()
function returns a file handle (which we discussed), which—preferably when bound to a variable—you use for all the remaining methods. There are two ways of writing this:
Plain Text
Copy
<handle> = open(<filename>)
​
Or:
Plain Text
Copy
with open(<filename>) as <handle>: <statements>
​
These two ways of writing code are semi-equivalent. The first way is a more classic way of writing things. However, the second method is more ‘Pythonic’ (i.e., what the Python community deems better practice), and has an advantage of automatically closing the file. However, seeing as we have not yet covered indentation and scopes, we’ll be using the first variant for now.
‼️
Note that in contrast to what we typically understand what it means to open a file (like open a file in VSCode, say),
open
does not actually give you the contents of a file like a word processor might. The variable it’s bound to is just a ‘file handling object’. This handler only tells Python where the file is, and what we want to do with it (read, write, etc.). Any
read
(getting the contents of the file) or
write
(writing something to the file) operation has its own methods associated, which we will discuss below.

🔎 Reading a File Using
read()

The simplest way to read the contents of a file and store the result in a variable is using the
read()
method (typically without arguments). This returns a string that contains the complete contents of the file. The one argument
read()
accepts relates to binary files, which we won’t use. The syntax of opening, reading, and storing the contents in a variable hence is as follows:
Plain Text
Copy
<handle> = open(<filename>) <file contents> = <handle>.read()Reading from a file moves the file pointer (see No access for more info) to right after the part of the file that was read. This means that if you use the
read()
method (without arguments), the file pointer is moved to the end of the file (see No access). This entails that if you would try to
read()
from it a second time, nothing would be read, as there is nothing to be read after the spot where the file pointer is.
​
Reading from a file moves the file pointer to right after the part of the file that was read. This means that if you use the
read()
method (without arguments), the file pointer is moved to the end of the file. This entails that if you would try to
read()
from it a second time, nothing would be read, as there is nothing to be read after the spot where the file pointer is.

🔒 Closing a File Using
close()

Every file that you open, you should close at some point in your program. Depending on the syntax you use to invoke the file handler, there are two ways to close a file after you’re done with it. Otherwise, it might potentially remain open forever, without any contents. We close like so:
Plain Text
Copy
<handle> = open(<filename>) <contents> = <handle>.read() <handle>.close() # do something with <contents> here
​
ℹ️
Note that
close()
simply closes the file handle. Its contents are saved in
<contents>
. Altering
<contents>
does not do anything to the actual file. For that, we would need to overwrite the original file with new content.

🖥️ Displaying the Contents of a File

Now the first few functions and methods for dealing with text files have been introduced, we can actually go over code that reads the contents of a file:
Python
Copy
fp = open("pc_rose.txt") in_buffer = fp.read() fp.close() # do not forget print(in_buffer)
​
This code assumes that a file is available with the name
pc_rose.txt
in the same directory as from where the code is run. For now, you can manually create this file. Simply make a new file in VSCode (File → New File → Text File), paste the contents below, and save it as
pc_rose.txt
. Double check you indeed named the file this way if it throws a
FileNotFoundError
.
Plain Text
Copy
'Tis but thy name that is my enemy. Thou art thyself, though not a Montague. What's Montague? it is nor hand, nor foot, Nor arm, nor face, nor any other part Belonging to a man. O, be some other name! What's in a name? That which we call a rose By any other name would smell as sweet. So Romeo would, were he not Romeo call'd, Retain that dear perfection which he owes Without that title. Romeo, doff thy name; And for that name, which is no part of thee, Take all myself.
​
💡
Please note that VSCode runs your code from the uppermost directory you have opened. As a result, files without any path will open/write in that directory. If you have subdirectories visible in VSCode that contain the
.py
file you are running, the above might not work. As an example, see below (note that
write_script.py
is in
subdir
):
You’ll have to read the 🗄️ Directories bonus content in that case. 🙂
💡
Windows might not show the
.txt
part, which might result in files being called
file.txt.txt
. Click the link to learn how to disable this behavior. MacOS does something similar, which can also be disabled.

📖 Opening a File for Writing

To open a file for writing, and writing only, you give the value
'w'
as the second argument to the
open()
function. If the file does not exist yet, it will create it.
‼️
If it does exist, it will delete its contents, so be careful with using this option willy-nilly. There is no warning message saying "are you sure?" The file is simply emptied. It’s therefore good practice to write your programs in such a way that they first check if a file exists before opening it for writing, and give an error message when it already exists. Functions for checking if a file exists are discussed later in this chapter.

✏️ Writing using
write()

To write something to a text file, you use the
write()
method with as argument a string that you want to write to the file. The example code below writes the given
str
to a file. It then opens the file, reads the contents, and displays them. Run the code and see what happens.
Python
Copy
a_long_string = "Hello this is just some example text."\ "We'll continue with our next sentence here."\ "Another line here." fp = open("pc_writetest.tmp", "w") fp.write(a_long_string) fp.close() # do NOT forget fp = open("pc_writetest.tmp") in_buffer = fp.read() fp.close() # do. not. forget. print(in_buffer)
​
After successful execution, you may have checked the file and noticed that all the text is there, but it all is on one line; i.e., there are no newlines (remember 💽Py2 - Data Types and Structures - 🚪 Escape Sequences) in between. Also, there are no spaces after the periods. You have to explicitly write newline characters when you want newlines in your file.
📍
Task: Change the code above so that every line of text is on a separate line in the file that you write back to disk. Should you add those previously missing spaces?

🕶️ Reading Lines Using
readlines()

Often we want to work on line level when dealing with files. The reason for this will become more obvious in later notebooks.
readlines()
reads all the lines in the file, and returns them as a
list
of
str
s. The strings include the newline characters:
Python
Copy
fp = open("pc_rose.txt") in_buffer = fp.readlines() fp.close() # seriously, do not forget print(in_buffer) first_line = in_buffer[0] print(first_line)
​

✒️ Writing using
writelines()

You can also write a
list
of
str
s at once, by using the
writelines()
method that gets the list as argument. Each of the strings in the list must end in a newline character if you want those newline characters in the output file.
writelines()
is the opposite of
readlines()
; if you use the collection that
readlines()
returns as argument for
writelines()
, the contents of the output file will be exactly the same as the contents of the input file. Note that there is no
writeline()
method.
writeline()
would be exactly the same method as
write()
, so it is not needed.
Python
Copy
list_of_vegetables = ["broccoli", "cucumber", "kale", "okra", "zucchini"] fp = open("veggie_list.tmp", "w") fp.writelines(list_of_vegetables) fp.close() # friends do not let friends leave their file handles open
​
📍

🧙‍♂️ Typecasting for Compatibility

As you may have noticed, the data types that we have discussed so far can in a sense all be written to file. However, in order to do so, they should all be converted to a
str
. Sure enough, whenever you do that, Python doesn’t complain: 
Python
Copy
my_int = 1 my_float = 0.00005 my_list = [1, 2, 3] my_dict = {'a': 1, 'b': 2} ifo = open('int_out.txt', 'w') ifo.write(str(my_int)) ifo.close() # 👀 ffo = open('float_out.txt', 'w') ffo.write(str(my_float)) ffo.close() # 👈 👀 flo = open('list_out.txt', 'w') flo.write(str(my_list)) flo.close() # 🔒 📁 👀 👍  fdo = open('dict_out.txt', 'w') fdo.write(str(my_dict)) fdo.close() # you get the gist
​
But what happens when we want to read these back? Let’s take the most annoying one as an example: the
dict
.
Python
Copy
fdi = open('dict_out.txt', 'r') our_dict = fdi.read() fdi.close() # :) print(our_dict) print(dict(our_dict))
​
We get an error! Seems like we need a better way to handle our data. Lucky for us, Python has these things, and the next section will discuss them.

🐼 Introduction to Pandas

Pandas (from ‘panel data’… s?) is a Python library designed to work with tabular data (two-dimensional structure where columns and rows have some meaning). This data can have a mixture of data types. It makes selection, processing, transformation, visualization, and advanced types of data analysis straight-forward and fast. It is particularly useful for grouping data, aggregating and processing these groups, and reshaping data. Support for time-series analyses in Pandas is also strong with built-in date and time representations.
Pandas should be installed on the campus computers. To get it yourself, you can follow the following steps:
Open up VSCode, click the cog (⚙️), and select ‘Command Palette’. Alternatively, you can press
Ctrl
(🪟) /
Cmd
(🍏) +
Shift
+
p
.
Type ‘Py term’ and the first option that will show up should be ‘Python: Create Terminal’. This will open up a terminal where the correct Python interpreter should be active.
In the terminal window (the thing that usually executes / shows your code), type the following:
python -m pip install pandas
. This tells
python
to call the module (
-m
) called
pip
, Python’s package installer (and a recursive acronym for ‘Pip Installs Packages’), and
install
the package
pandas
.
You can test if this all worked by writing a script that starts with the following:
Python
Copy
import pandas as pd
​
This does two things:
It imports a library / package. Meaning the Python interpreter now knows we want to use the codebase of Pandas in our current project. This
pd
variable with now offer a whole bunch of methods and functions. See for reference only (you don’t need to know all of these):
API reference — pandas 2.3.2 documentation
This page gives an overview of all public pandas objects, functions and methods. All classes and functions exposed in pandas.* namespace are public.
https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/reference/index.html
The second part, is an ‘alias’. It tells Python that we’d like to shorthand pandas to
pd
. Why? Simple as that your lines will be shorter, and you don’t have to write
pandas.something()
all the time, and can simply type
pd.something()
. The
pd
alias is an accepted standard, like
numpy
has
np
and
pytorch
has
pt
, for example.

📦 Data Structures

You know about basic data types by now. Pandas introduces two data structures:
Series
, an equivalent to
list
s, and
DataFrame
s, an equivalent to
dict
s or a
list
of
list
s, depending on how you look at it. List of what now? Let’s first talk about some advanced ways of using our data types before we continue.

🗄️ Storing Complicated Values

Until now we only considered flat
list
s and
dict
s that store a single entry per
key
/
value
— both of a simple data type. We know that
list
s can contain
int
s,
float
s,
str
s, or everything at once:
Python
Copy
some_valid_list = ["fruit", 0, 0.5]
​
But lists can also house other
list
s, or even
dict
s!
Python
Copy
another_valid_list = ["fruit", 0, 0.5, ["this", "is", "a", "nested", "list"], 1]
​
Wowza. Anything to note here? Yes, our top list has index, but so does the nested list!
index
0
1
2
3
4
top list element
"fruit"
0
0.5
["this", "is", "a", "nested", "list"]
1
nested list element
"this"
"is"
"a"
"nested"
"list"
How do we access the elements of the nested list? Through double indexing notation. So:
Python
Copy
another_valid_list = ["fruit", 0, 0.5, ["this", "is", "a", "nested", "list"], 1] print(another_valid_list[0]) # "fruit" print(another_valid_list[3]) # the nested list print(another_valid_list[3][0]) # "this"
​
ℹ️
For those who practiced NumPy (through e.g. the bootcamps or the ‘advanced’ track): note that this syntax is different!
some_array[0, 0]
is the same as
some_list[0][0]
.
As we very briefly covered last chapter, we can store such complex objects in
dict
s as well! A
key
should at least be immutable (meaning that in addition to simple
int
,
float
,
str
keys,
tuple
s are valid too — as long as it’s stably hashable). The
values
can hold anything. Below a
dict
is used to store the courses, and the students that follow them. The course is identified by its course number, while the students are identified by their student numbers:
Python
Copy
courses = { '880254': ['u123456', 'u383213', 'u234178'], '822177': ['u123456', 'u223416', 'u234178'], '822164': ['u123456', 'u223416', 'u383213', 'u234178'] } print(courses["822164"]) print(courses["822164"][0]) print(courses["822164"][0:2]) print(courses["822164"][-1])
​
Suppose that we do not only want to store the student numbers for a course number, but also the name of the course, the ECTS value of the course, and for each student number also the grade. You can do that (for example) by storing the value for a course number as a
dict
, with three
keys
, namely
"name"
,
"ects"
, and
"students"
. The value for
"name"
is the course name as a
str
, the value for
"ects"
is the ECTS as an
int
, and the value for
"students"
is another
dict
, which contains student numbers as
keys
and grades as
values
.
Python
Copy
courses = { '880254': { "name": "Research Skills: Data Processing", "ects": 3, "students": { 'u123456': 8, 'u383213': 7.5, 'u234178': 6 } }, '822177': { "name": "Understanding Intelligence", "ects": 6, "students": { 'u123456': 5, 'u223416': 7, 'u234178': 9 } }, '822164': { "name": "Computer Games", "ects": 6, "students": { 'u123456': 7.5, 'u223416': 9, 'u383213': 6, 'u234178': 4 } } } print(courses['822177']) print(courses['822177']['name']) print(courses['822177']['students']) print(courses['822177']['students']['u123456'])
​
Knowing all of this, it’s easier to see how these kind of structures relate to stuff in Pandas!
🤖
Data Science Example: Now that we’ve delved into
dict
s with complex structures, we have basically covered JSON files. They have the same syntax and formatting, with possible
int
s,
float
s,
str
s,
list
s, and more
dict
s (no special Python objects like
tuple
s or
set
s though!). You can read and write
dict
s to JSON files in several ways. The most common way is to save each data entry as one JSON object on each line. However, the easiest one is to let the
json
library handle everything:
Python
Copy
import json courses = { '880254': { "name": "Programming for Data Science", "ects": 5, "students": { 'u123456': 8, 'u383213': 7.5, 'u234178': 6 } }, '822177': { "name": "Programming & Algorithmic Thinking", "ects": 6, "students": { 'u123456': 5, 'u223416': 7, 'u234178': 9 } }, '822164': { "name": "Research Skill: Reproducibility & Model Deployment", "ects": 3, "students": { 'u123456': 7.5, 'u223416': 9, 'u383213': 6, 'u234178': 4 } } } fo = open('courses.json', 'w') json.dump(courses, fo) fo.close() fi = open('courses.json', 'r') new_courses = json.load(fi) fi.close() print(new_courses)
​
For saving,
json.dump()
takes a
dict
as the first argument, and a file buffer set to write as the second argument. For loading,
json.load()
takes a file buffer set to read as the only argument. These work similar to
write()
and
read()
respectively, but given that they aren’t methods of the
open()
file buffer, you have to pass this to the function itself.

🎨
Series

The basic data structure in Pandas is a
Series
, which consists of:
The data. This looks list a
list
. All elements have to be of the same type. For those in the advanced track: it’s a
numpy
one-dimensional array of elements, hence the type restriction.
A mapping of indexes (can be
int
s or
str
). This looks like a
dict
. For those in the advanced track: these map to positions within the
numpy
array.
Some additional header information.
A simple test:
Python
Copy
import pandas as pd data = pd.Series([1, 2, 3]) print(data)
​

🖼️
DataFrame

The most used data structure in Pandas is a
DataFrame
. It contains two dimensions: every column is a
Series
object, and every column has the same number of elements (rows).
DataFrame
s are actually stored as a Python
dict
(with some additional header information). The
key
in this
dict
indicates the column name, and the
value
is the Pandas
Series
.
🧠
There are some advantages and disadvantages to how Pandas structures memory. First, by default each column is a
numpy
array, so computations within each column are very fast. Second, by having a dedicated and reasonably fast data structure (the
dict
) to connect row indexes, computations across rows are reasonably fast too. However, by storing additional index information for every column (it isn't really that bad, but is definitely extra) additional memory is needed to store a pandas DataFrame relative to a
numpy
multi-dimensional array with the same number of elements. There is also the option to store most types as a
pyarrow
array, which is faster and memory efficient.
Another simple test:
Python
Copy
import pandas as pd data = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]) print(data)
​
Notice how a
list
of
list
s can be seen as equivalent to a table (or matrix):
[123456]\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \end{bmatrix}[14​25​36​]
You can see the indices (0, 1 for rows; and 0, 1, 2 for columns) in the print output as well.

🖌️ Creating and Populating
DataFrame
s

⚠️
For brevity, from here on, you can assume
import pandas as pd
is on top of every code cell. If you see
NameError: name 'pd' is not defined
, you forgot to add it.
So how do we arrive at a proper structure? There are a few options, one is pretending like we have everything accessible in
list
s. While not often used in practice, it’s useful to know how to construct an empty, or minimal
DataFrame
with the appropriately named columns, so we may start adding to it. A simple empty example with columns would be:
Python
Copy
df = pd.DataFrame([], columns=['some_col_name', 'another_col_name']) print(df)
​
So what’s going on here? Before, we provided a
list
as the only input. However, the
DataFrame
data structure has parameters! We can also provide what the columns should be called (otherwise, they just receive a simple index). If we then want to add data, that’s possible like so:
Python
Copy
df = pd.DataFrame([], columns=['some_col_name', 'another_col_name']) df['some_col_name'] = [1] print(df)
​
Notice that we only set one ‘cell’; the first value for the first row for the column
some_col_name
. The value on that row for
another_col_name
is empty, and shows
NaN
(Not a Number,
<NA>
).
📍
Task: Set a value for
another_col_name
on the first row as well.
📍
Task: How would we go about adding two rows? Hint: it only requires minor changes to the code we already have.

🗃️ From a
list

So we already practiced with
list
input a bit. Let’s try a bit more of an expansive example, with a
list
of
list
s:
Python
Copy
# creating a list of lists, includes NaN students_info = [['Anna', 'van Rossum', 'F', 92, 9.0, True], ['David', 'Alberts', 'M', 'NaN', 'NaN', False], ['Ibrahim', 'Assad', 'M', 76, 7.5, True], ['Maria', 'Esposito', 'F', 43, 4.0, False], ['Sophie', 'van Hee', 'F', 84, 8.5, True]] # creating a list of index labels student_numbers = [42343, 23423, 57567, 54644, 34534] column_labels = ['Name', 'Surname', 'Gender', 'Marks', 'Grade', 'Pass'] pfds_grades = pd.DataFrame(data=students_info, index=student_numbers, columns=column_labels) print(pfds_grades)
​
Note that we pass a custom
index
, and that the data includes empty values (coded as a string:
'NaN'
, which
pandas
detects automagically). Our
data
also resembles a matrix / table here, with every row in a new
list
nested within a
list
.

🗃️ From a
dict

Perhaps a slightly more intuitive input example is using a
dict
, where now rather than row-wise, our data is now formatted column-wise: they
key
s are the column names, and the
values
a list with the entries within that column.
Python
Copy
pfds_grades = { "Name": ["Anna", "David", "Ibrahim", "Maria", "Sophie"], "Surname": ["van Rossum", "Alberts", "Assad", "Esposito", "van Hee"], "Gender": ["F", "M", "M", "F", "F"], "Marks": [92, 'NaN', 76, 43, 84], "Grade": [9.0, 'NaN', 7.5, 4.0, 8.5], "Pass": [True, False, True, False, True], } student_numbers = [42343, 23423, 57567, 54644, 34534] df = pd.DataFrame(pfds_grades, index=student_numbers) print(df)
​

📁 From Files

Python
Copy
# paste this below one of the scripts above df.to_csv('pfds_grades.csv') df = pd.read_csv('pfds_grades.csv', index_col=0) print(df)
​
📍
Task: Create your own
.csv
file in an empty text file in VSCode. The first line is the header, with columns separated by comma’s. The second line are the values (also comma-separated); make sure these match the amount of columns. Now, open the file in
pandas
. If it doesn’t work, or look right, compare your file with
pfds_grades.csv
.
Other input and output:
IO tools (text, CSV, HDF5, …) — pandas 2.3.2 documentation
The pandas I/O API is a set of top level reader functions accessed like pd.read_csv() that generally return a pandas object. The corresponding writer functions are object methods that are accessed like DataFrame.to_csv(). Below is a table containing available readers and writers.
https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/user_guide/io.html#io

🧰 Simple DataFrame Attributes and Methods

In the list below, not everything is a method. Some are properties of the
DataFrame
itself, and hence do not need to be called. These are called attributes, and typically simply retrieve some information about the
DataFrame
that’s already stored in the data structure (e.g. the amount of columns, the data types, etc.).
index
columns
dtypes
info()
head()
and
tail()
drop()
sort_values()
sample()
In addition to this,
DataFrames
has attributes and methods you’re already familiar with from other data structures, but that at times work slightly differently; for example,
copy()
,
keys()
(gives the column names),
values
(gives the table cells),
insert()
(inserts a column at a particular index, with
<index, column name, column values>
as parameters), and
pop()
(removes
<column name>
).
📍
Task: Practice with sorting in place (
inplace=True
) and not in place (
inplace=False
). Make sure to
print()
the variables you store the output in, if any, and the original
DataFrame
. Can you see the difference?

🔢 Indexing
DataFrame
s

As with any data structure, it is important to be able to access subsets of the
DataFrame
. Pandas has a number of methods for accessing both rows and columns in a number of ways.

🎨 With Attributes

First, you can access a single, complete column from a
DataFrame
as an attribute. This method will return a
Series
object (one column from the
DataFrame
), and can only work when the attribute has a legal
str
name:
df.1
is an
int
, and is therefore invalid even if there is a column named
1
in data,
df.min
is invalid even if a column is named
min
as it conflicts with the method
min()
.
Note that capitalization in the column names needs to be included:
Python
Copy
df = pd.read_csv('pfds_grades.csv', index_col=0) print(df.Grade)
​

🕴️Matrix Indexing

Much like
list
s and
dict
s, the
[]
notation can be used for indexing columns and rows. For columns, you can specify a single column name (like with
dict
s). If you want to select multiple, it needs to a nested
list
(this does not work for
dict
s):
Python
Copy
df = pd.read_csv('pfds_grades.csv', index_col=0) print(df['Marks']) # returns a series print(df[['Marks', 'Grade']]) # returns a dataframe
​
When using the
[]
notation to index rows by their index, you (somewhat surprisingly) cannot specify a single index, you must specify a slice (see 💽Py2 - Data Types and Structures - 🗂️ Indexing for a refresher):
Python
Copy
df = pd.read_csv('pfds_grades.csv', index_col=0) print(df[0:1]) print(df[0:2])
​

🏷️ By Label and Location

The
.loc
attribute can be used to index:
a single row with a specified index,
multiple rows,
multiple rows and columns.
It’s label-based, meaning that instead of grabbing data by position (like a list index: 
a_list[0]
), you grab it by the row and column labels (so closer to how a
dict
works). When a single label is specified, it is assumed to be an index label (so a row):
Python
Copy
df = pd.read_csv('pfds_grades.csv', index_col=0) print(df.loc[57567]) print(df.loc[34534:57567])
​
So for now, it kind of looks like what we had before without
loc
, so why are we covering this? You can be super specific about the exact index + column combinations you want to select. Subsetting a columns for all indices requires including the full range of rows
:
and the comma:
Python
Copy
df = pd.read_csv('pfds_grades.csv', index_col=0) print(df.loc[:,['Name', 'Grade', 'Pass']])
​
So in a sense, it combines the two ways of indexing we saw before! However, with
loc
, we can provide both ranges of indices, and ranges of columns!
Python
Copy
df = pd.read_csv('pfds_grades.csv', index_col=0) print(df.loc[54644:34534, 'Name':'Grade'])
​
The
.iloc
attribute can be used to index on location. This can be done via:
a single position (e.g.
14
,
2
),
a list of positions (
[1, 3, 2]
),
a slice (
3:42
) (only lower is included, upper is excluded — this is different than
loc
!).
Python
Copy
df = pd.read_csv('pfds_grades.csv', index_col=0) print(df.iloc[3]) print(df.iloc[3, 2]) # Selection by index for rows print(df.iloc[3:5, 0:5]) # Selection by index for rows and columns print(df.iloc[3:5, [1,3,5]])
​

📦 By Data Type

We can use
select_dtypes
function to retrieve columns with certain data types, for example:
To select all numeric types, use
'number'
,
To select
str
s, use the
'string'
dtype,
To select Pandas categorical dtypes, use
'category'
.
Python
Copy
df = pd.read_csv('pfds_grades.csv', index_col=0) only_numericals = df.select_dtypes(include=['number']) no_strings = df.select_dtypes(exclude=['string']) only_strings = df.select_dtypes(include=['string']) print(only_numericals) print(no_strings) print(only_strings)
​

🔬 Preview Advanced Combinations

⚠️
This subsection (i.e., discussing
describe()
and
groupby()
) is not part of the midterm material.
We’ll dedicate much more space to these in the upcoming weeks. However, to give you a small taste of what Pandas can be used for other than just storing and manipulating data, here are some useful methods.

📊 Getting Stats Through
describe()

The
describe()
method provides descriptive statistics of all numeric columns in a
DataFrame
. You can think of it as a stats cheat; it looks at your data and automatically calculates the most common summary numbers:
For numeric columns: count, mean, standard deviation, min, quartiles, max.
For non-numeric columns: count, number of unique values, most frequent value, etc.
See below:
Python
Copy
df = pd.read_csv('pfds_grades.csv', index_col=0) print(df.describe())
​
To include non-numeric values, we have to be explicit:
Python
Copy
df = pd.read_csv('pfds_grades.csv', index_col=0) print(df.describe(include='object'))
​
The output of the
describe()
function is also a
DataFrame
:
Python
Copy
df = pd.read_csv('pfds_grades.csv', index_col=0) desc = df.describe() print(desc.info())
​
This can be used as a quick ‘health check’ of your
DataFrame
and makes for an ideal Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) partner: do I have any outliers? Is much data missing? It helps detect anomalies, skewness, or imbalance.

🗜️ Aggregating Values Through
groupby()

Where 
.describe()
 provides summaries across the dataset as a whole, 
.groupby()
 allows you to partition a dataset into subgroups:
df.groupby(<col>)
 — returns a
groupby
object for values from one column,
df.groupby([<col1>, <col2>])
 — returns a
groupby
object values from multiple columns.
Conceptually, 
groupby()
 implements what Hadley Wickham (in R terminology) called the split–apply–combine pattern:
Split: divide the dataset into groups based on the values of one or more keys (e.g., “pass”).
Apply: apply a function (e.g.
count()
) to each group independently.
Combine: aggregate the results into a new
DataFrame
or
Series
for inspection.
Source: files.codingninjas.in.
ALT
Python
Copy
pfds_grades = { "Name": ["Anna", "Ibrahim", "Maria", "Sophie"], "Surname": ["van Rossum", "Assad", "Esposito", "van Hee"], "Gender": ["F", "M", "F", "F"], "Marks": [92, 76, 43, 84], "Grade": [9.0, 7.5, 4.0, 8.5], "Pass": [True, True, False, True], "Track": ['Advanced', 'Main', 'Main', 'Main'] } student_numbers = [42343, 23423, 57567, 54644] df = pd.DataFrame(pfds_grades, index=student_numbers) g = df.groupby('Pass') print(g.groups)
​

📈 Combining
describe()
and
groupby()

Together, these two methods form a foundation for EDA: we begin with an overall statistical fingerprint (
describe()
), and then refine our view by splitting the data into meaningful subsets (
groupby()
). Here we can see grade stats by track:
Python
Copy
# use df above print(df.groupby(['Track']).describe()['Grade'])
​

🧙 Converting Output to Python

Many of the methods we discuss produce a
pandas
-compatible object, but those aren’t always nice to work with in other bits of code. Luckily, Pandas provides typecasting tools, and some Python variants work as well, for example:
Python
Copy
df = pd.read_csv('pfds_grades.csv', index_col=0) print(list(df.columns)) print(list(df.dtypes.astype(str)))
​

⭐ Bonus Content

🗄️ Directories

As you might have noticed, we were pretty strict with “make sure the file is in the same directory as the code”. Directories (dirs), or folders, we assume most of you are familiar with (if not, you might want to use a search engine to inform you). More of you might not be familiar with the fact that default directories provided by operating systems, like Documents and Downloads, are also in a directory. Same goes for the directory that belongs to you: or rather, your user account. You might have noticed when executing code in VSCode that it gives two paths:
Plain Text
Copy
/Path/to/anaconda3/bin/python /Dir/from/which/you/are/executing/your_code.py
​
ℹ️
If you’re on Windows, the slashes might show as backslashes (e.g.,
\User\you\etc.
).
The first one might have an alias (e.g. just say
python
); however, if not, it points to the directory where Python (or more accurately its executable) is located. The second one gives the full path of the file, starting at the top most directory. This is typically a drive letter on Windows, like
C:
, and a
/
(also called the root directory) on Unix systems (i.e., MacOS and Linux). Every subsequent part that’s delimited by a
/
or
\
is a directory down (subdirectories).
Let’s suppose you are working in
C:\Users\<yourname>\Documents\rsdp\week-4
or
Users/<yourname>/Documents/rsdp/week-4
, you will see this full path and then
<filename>.py
. This is called the ‘current working directory’; the directory you execute your code from (namely,
week-4
). The directory that contains
week-4
(i.e.,
rsdp
) is called its “parent directory”.
You can open a file using a “relative path” to its directory, meaning you tell Python where to go from the current directory (say: go back one directory, then down into
text_files
). Alternatively, you can open using an “absolute path”, which would be the full
C:\<bunch of directories>\rsdp\week-4\filename.py
shown above. To pass ‘absolute’ directory names when opening files in Python, they need to be formatted in this exact way. For ‘relative’ directory names, there are a few pieces of syntax to know:
/
— starting with
/
always means “root”, which is the topmost directory (on Unix systems).
./
— a period before a directory delimiter means “from the current directory”.
../
— two periods before a directory delimiter means “go one directory back” (or up).
So let’s suppose we have the following file structure:
Plain Text
Copy
rsdp |____ week-1 | |_______ hello-world.py | |_______ testing.py |____ week-4 | |_______ myscript.py |____ pcdata |_______ pc_amontillado.txt |_______ pc_rose.txt |_______ pc_writetest.tmp
​
This indicates
rsdp
is a directory (we don’t show whatever the parent directory or higher order directories are here), which contains three directories:
week-1
,
week-4
, and
pcdata
. These then hold a few files each; for example, the
pc_
files are in
pcdata
. Let’s suppose we’d want to open
pc_rose.txt
in the
myscript.py
file (that is in a different directory). Opening this file using a relative path would look like:
Python
Copy
print(open('../pcdata/pc_rose.txt').read())
​
So, to reiterate:
The current working directory is
week-4
(that’s where
myscript.py
is).
We tell Python to ‘go back one directory’:
../
.
This means it then is back in
rsdp
(that’s the parent directory).
We then tell it to look in
pcdata
:
../pcdata/
.
And at the end we need to add the file we want to open:
'../pcdata/pc_rose.txt'
.
📍
Task: Create the file structure as shown above (you can ignore
week-1
if you want to). You can do this from within VSCode (check the instruction video if you’re unsure how to). You can do this using Python too, but you can ignore that for this course. Move the files you created in the last few examples to the
pcdata
directory. Add the code above in
myscript.py
and run the script. Now try to find the absolute path. Tip: right clicking a file or directory in VSCode gives you two ‘copy path’ options that will add something to your clipboard, which you might want to try pasting somewhere.

🗃️ File Encoding

This section used to be longer, but you really only need to know that certain encodings exist of various character sets. Those encodings might give errors if you don’t tell Python what the encoding of a file actually is. Remember that an "encoding" is a system that prescribes how characters in the files are supposed to be interpreted. The same goes for fancy symbols we use such as á, æ, ♬, ⛬, and even 💩. This encoding may differ between operating systems. You can see the preferred encoding that your system uses with a call to
sys.getfilesystemencoding()
.
Python
Copy
from sys import getfilesystemencoding print(getfilesystemencoding())
​
These encodings date back to a time where US developers only encoded files in ASCII; i.e., alphanumerical (a-z, 0-9) characters, perhaps a symbol or two. This initially included none of the characters used in other languages. If you speak any other language than English, you know that ignoring them doesn’t always work out very well in communication.
If you read a text file which uses a different encoding than your file system prefers, you may get a
UnicodeDecodeError
. Whether or not you get this error for a particular file, is related to your operating system, and the way the file was initially encoded. An annoying consequence of that is that when you port Python code that reads a file to another system, a file that could be read by your code previously may cause your code to crash after the port.
An easy way to get around this problem is by adding an extra parameter when opening a file, which indicates the encoding mechanism that should be used when reading the file. You do this by adding a parameter
encoding=<encodingname>
to
open()
, where
<encodingname>
is a string that can have a variety of values, for which some typical ones are:
Plain Text
Copy
ascii 7-bits encoding, supports characters with values in the range 00-7F latin-1 8-bits encoding, supports characters with values in the range 00-FF mbcs 2-byte encoding, that is currently getting replaced by UTF-8 utf-8 variable bytes encoding
​
In many applications,
'utf8'
is the widely used standard, sometimes
'utf-16'
. Web data in particular (🤖 Data Science Example) is pretty notorious for having random encodings to their web pages that your browser happily makes sense of, but once you download/scrape that data, you will undoubtedly run into encoding errors at some point.
